name: Eastern Abenaki
sweep_summary: Eastern Abenaki (Penobscot) is not in the catalog. The single sweep item, Siebert 1988 'The suprasegmental phonemes of the Penobscot dialect of Eastern Abenaki' (In Honor of Mary Haas, 715-764, DOI 10.1515/9783110852387.715), is the source of record but remains paywalled (De Gruyter; archive.org copy lending-restricted with a 401 text layer; not in HathiTrust/Google Books) — priority high; Harvard HOLLIS has online access per the audit. Read in this sweep: Voorhis 1979 (open PDF found on University of Manitoba MSpace, hdl 1993/18305, previously marked print-only) gives the only first-hand accent statement — accent is a phoneme with 'frequent variation in the place of accent', lexically fixed on many noun stems and shifted by certain suffixes; verb-stem accents 'too uncertain to be indicated' (pp. 12, 64-65). Open Algonquian Conference papers add second-hand pieces of Siebert's system: Quinn 1999:291 relays Siebert 1988:729 (in open penultimate syllables all vowels except schwa lengthen to four moras); Siebert 1988 Tag-questions describes three phrase-level intonation prosodemes and tonic/atonic primary accent; Quinn 2001 notes high vs. low accent and that accent normally falls within the last few syllables. Speck 1918 marks stress but states no rule; Rasles 1833 and O'Brien 1887 (Norridgewock dialect) give nothing. Not obtained: Quinn 2006 Harvard dissertation (ProQuest only), Quinn's 'Reader Guide to the Penobscot Language' in Still They Remember Me (2021, JSTOR/MUSE, pp. 47-52; likely a plain statement of the accent marks), Siebert's unpublished dictionary introduction, Goddard 1978 (HNAI 15). Bing/DDG/Brave/Mojeek/Yahoo/Startpage/CORE/BASE/Semantic Scholar/OpenAlex/fatcat were blocked or rate-limited, so discovery relied on Crossref, archive.org, Open Library, OJS, MSpace and Wikipedia APIs. new_statements.quote: There is frequent variation in the place of accent; the few discernable patterns are subject to many exceptions: [...] Many stems seem to have a basic accent on a certain syllable, and the accent tends to remain on that syllable throughout inflexion: awás 'beast' (2.27) / awássvk 'animals' (2.18) / awássətok 'animals' (vocative) (2.16) [...] Certain suffixes, however, cause the accent to change; for example, in noun inflexion, the accent often shifts to the syllable preceding -m-, -ənaw-, and -owy-, see below.
new_statements.citation: Voorhis, Paul H. (1979). Grammatical Notes on the Penobscot Language from Frank Speck's Penobscot Transformer Tales. Winnipeg: Department of Anthropology, University of Manitoba. Section 2 Phonology.
new_statements.locator: p. 12 (PDF page 15); cf. p. 11 and pp. 64-65
new_statements.reading: Voorhis finds no positional stress rule in Speck's 1918 Penobscot texts: accent is treated as a phoneme, is lexically fixed on a stem syllable for many nouns and persists through inflection, but is shifted by certain suffixes, and for verbs 'the basic accents of verb stems, if there are any, are too uncertain to be indicated' (pp. 64-65). This is a secondary analysis of Speck's non-phonemic transcription, not fieldwork; Siebert's own analysis (1988, paywalled) treats Penobscot as having phonemic suprasegmentals (tonic vs. atonic primary accent, high vs. low accent, penultimate lengthening of non-schwa vowels in open syllables per Quinn 1999:291) and supersedes Voorhis. Reading for a catalog entry: lexically/morphologically determined accent (pitch-accent-like), not a fixed-position word stress; provisional until Siebert 1988 is read.

sources.quote: There is frequent variation in the place of accent; the few discernable patterns are subject to many exceptions: [...] Many stems seem to have a basic accent on a certain syllable, and the accent tends to remain on that syllable throughout inflexion: awás 'beast' (2.27) / awássvk 'animals' (2.18) / awássətok 'animals' (vocative) (2.16) [...] Certain suffixes, however, cause the accent to change; for example, in noun inflexion, the accent often shifts to the syllable preceding -m-, -ənaw-, and -owy-, see below.
sources.locator: p. 12 (PDF page 15); also p. 11 (PDF p. 14) and pp. 64-65 (PDF p. 67-68)
sources.note: Section 2 Phonology (pp. 3-12) lists 'Accent' as a phoneme and retranscribes Speck's acute/grave as a single accent. p. 12: accent placement in Speck's texts varies; no positional rule is found; many stems have a lexically fixed 'basic accent' that persists under inflection, but certain suffixes shift it (to the syllable preceding -m-, -ənaw-, -owy- in noun inflection). p. 64-65: 'The basic accents of verb stems, if there are any, are too uncertain to be indicated.' Based entirely on Speck 1918's transcription, not on Voorhis's own fieldwork; predates Siebert's phonemic analysis.

sources.citation: Quinn, Conor (2001). A preliminary survey of animacy categories in Penobscot. Papers of the Algonquian Conference 32: 395-426.
sources.quote: This too is either a typo, or the only word in the entire Penobscot lexicon to be stressed five full syllables from the end and use the locative suffix /-ək/ to mark the animate plural.
sources.note: Not about stress; incidental remarks only: fn. 14 'Word-initial high stress on a schwa is unusual for Siebert-transcribed Penobscot'; fn. 29 'the accented syllable does not match the usual pattern of Penobscot words'; fn. 31 a suspect entry would be 'the only word in the entire Penobscot lexicon to be stressed five full syllables from the end'; p. 403 'the low accent on nəkətakʷ is not the expected nəkátakʷ'. These imply accent is normally within the last few syllables and that high vs. low accent is distinguished, but state no rule.

sources.citation: Quinn, Conor (1999). Some unresolved issues in the Penobscot materials of Frank T. Siebert, Jr. Papers of the Algonquian Conference 30: 288-297.
sources.quote: Further complicating the matter is that the morphemes involving schwa and h often occur in the penultimate syllable; as Siebert (1988:729) has explained, in open penultimate syllables all Penobscot vowels except schwa are lengthened to four moras. [...] An exception to the general pattern of open-penultimate vowel lengthening is precisely when the vowel precedes h. This exception is not mentioned in his article on Penobscot suprasegmentals (Siebert 1988), but Siebert told me so on one occasion
sources.note: Explicitly excludes the suprasegmentals ('I have intentionally excluded from this paper questions regarding the transcription of Penobscot's suprasegmental phonemes, because their complexity requires a discussion of its own', p. 288), but relays Siebert 1988:729 on penultimate lengthening (open penult: all vowels except schwa lengthen to four moras; not before h per Siebert p.c.). Useful as the only open pointer into Siebert 1988's content.

sources.citation: Siebert, Frank T. (1988). Tag-questions in Penobscot. Papers of the Algonquian Conference 19: 187-190.
sources.quote: In the Penobscot dialect of Eastern Abenaki ordinary interrogation is indicated by one of the three suprasegmental phonemes of intonation (or prosodemes) whose domain is the phrase. [...] Also, the interrogative prosodeme is often associated with mutations of the accompanying suprasegmentals of primary accent, changing them from atonic to tonic. All the details of ordinary interrogation are described in full elsewhere (Siebert 1988).
sources.note: Sentence intonation: three phrase-level intonation prosodemes; interrogative intonation raises the final syllable a major second to major third and is 'often associated with mutations of the accompanying suprasegmentals of primary accent, changing them from atonic to tonic'; defers word accent details to Siebert 1988 (Haas volume).

sources.citation: Siebert, Frank T. (1980). The Penobscot dictionary project: preferences and problems of format, presentation, and entry. Papers of the Algonquian Conference 11: 113-127.
sources.quote: (7) Effect of Adjacent Sounds and Suprasegmentals. Schwa (ə) in open syllables before a sibilant and following a checked syllable or an accented tonic syllable is syncopated.
sources.note: About lexicography and syncope; notes that the Jesuit records fail to mark 'suprasegmentals which are phonemic' (p. 115) and that syncope of schwa is conditioned by 'an accented tonic syllable' (p. 126). No statement of where accent falls.
